issues.legal_issue: Review of a professional-misconduct finding is limited to exceptional grounds and does not ordinarily permit reappraisal of evidence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged a High Court order finding an advocate guilty of professional misconduct and suspending him from practice.
The High Court had considered the inquiry report and evidence, including the credibility of a witness said to support the advocate’s defence.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court would not reappraise the evidence or revisit factual findings absent an exceptional ground such as a question of principle, a breach of natural justice, or a miscarriage of justice.
issues.legal_principle: The High Court has primary responsibility under section 10 of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926, to maintain professional standards. The Supreme Court’s jurisdiction in an appeal under Article 136 is exercised with great reluctance in such matters and ordinarily does not extend to reappraising evidence. Interference may be warranted in exceptional cases involving a question of principle, violation of natural justice, or miscarriage of justice. The jurisdiction is neither civil nor criminal in the sense used in Articles 133 and 134 of the Constitution.

predicates.appeal_from_professional_misconduct_orde: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an order made in a professional-misconduct matter.
predicates.exceptional_review_ground_absent: The record discloses no exceptional question of principle, breach of natural justice, or miscarriage of justice.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a professional-misconduct order and no exceptional review ground is present, the Supreme Court does not reappraise the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of an express recital of consultation with the professional council does not by itself invalidate a reference for inquiry, and a factual challenge not raised below may be declined.
material_facts: The High Court referred the professional-misconduct matter to a District Judge for inquiry under section 10(2) of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926.
The reference order did not expressly state that the Bar Council had been consulted.
The advocate did not raise the consultation objection in the High Court, including when seeking a certificate to appeal.
Whether consultation had occurred was a question of fact.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to entertain the objection, held that the absence of an express statement in the reference order was not decisive, and applied a presumption of regularity to official and judicial acts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2) of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926, provides for reference to a District Judge after consultation with the Bar Council. The Court assumed, without deciding, that consultation was mandatory. Official and judicial acts are presumed regular, and the party challenging regularity must plead and prove the contrary. The Court declined to entertain this factual objection because it had not been raised below.

predicates.professional_discipline_reference_to_inq: A professional-misconduct matter is referred by a court to another court or judge for inquiry.
predicates.reference_order_omits_consultation_state: The reference order does not expressly record that consultation with the professional council occurred.
predicates.consultation_objection_not_raised_below: The party challenging the reference did not raise the consultation issue before the court that made or considered the reference.

issues.definition: If a professional-misconduct reference omits an express statement of consultation and the consultation objection was not raised below, the objection is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge based on the form of a complaint does not invalidate disciplinary proceedings where the complaint was properly signed and verified, and the court could also initiate proceedings on its own motion.
material_facts: The complainants filed a fresh petition after a defect in the original petition’s attestation was identified.
The fresh petition was signed and verified by the complainants before the District Judge, who attested their signatures.
The High Court was competent under section 10(2) of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926, to initiate proceedings on its own motion.
issues.conclusion: The complaint-form objection was rejected because the complaint was signed and verified; in any event, the High Court could initiate the proceedings on its own motion.
issues.legal_principle: The proceedings were treated as proceedings under section 10(2) of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926. The complaint was signed and verified in accordance with the applicable High Court rules. The Court also held that the objection lacked substance because the High Court had power under section 10(2) to initiate proceedings suo motu.

predicates.professional_discipline_proceeding: The matter is a court proceeding to determine whether a legal practitioner committed professional misconduct.
predicates.complaint_properly_signed_and_verified: The complainants signed the complaint and affirmed its contents in the required manner.
predicates.court_can_initiate_proceeding_on_own_mot: The court has authority to commence the professional-misconduct proceeding without a formally sufficient complaint from a complainant.

issues.definition: In a professional-discipline proceeding, a complaint-form objection does not invalidate the proceeding when the complaint is properly signed and verified or the court may initiate the proceeding on its own motion.

issues.legal_issue: A court may proceed directly with professional-discipline proceedings for misconduct closely connected to a practitioner’s duty to a client, even if the conduct may also constitute a criminal offence.
material_facts: The advocate received money belonging to clients in the course of representing them in litigation.
The allegation was that he did not pay the money to the clients despite demand and falsely claimed to have paid it.
The alleged misconduct arose directly from the advocate’s relationship and duty to his clients.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was justified in proceeding under the professional-discipline jurisdiction rather than requiring the clients to pursue a criminal prosecution first.
issues.legal_principle: Proceedings under section 10 of the Indian Bar Councils Act, 1926, are directed to maintaining professional discipline and determining whether a practitioner is fit to continue in the profession; criminal proceedings seek to enforce the criminal law and punish an offender. Whether to proceed directly with discipline proceedings or await a criminal case is a matter of discretion depending on the circumstances. Where misconduct is connected with the practitioner’s duty to a client, the court may properly proceed directly. Chandi Charan Mitter, a Pleader, In re (1920) and Emperor v. Satish Chandra Singha (1927) were distinguished because the alleged misconduct there was not similarly connected to the practitioner’s immediate professional relationship with a client. Stephens v. Hills (1842) was referred to in support of the distinction between misconduct connected with professional duties and other misconduct.

predicates.professional_discipline_proceeding: The matter is a proceeding to determine whether a practitioner should be permitted to continue in the profession.
predicates.misconduct_may_be_criminal: The alleged conduct may also amount to an offence under ordinary criminal law.
predicates.misconduct_directly_connected_to_client_: The alleged conduct arose directly from the practitioner’s handling of a client’s affairs or property in the professional relationship.

issues.definition: When potentially criminal conduct is directly connected to a client duty, a court hearing a professional-discipline proceeding may proceed directly with that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: The order in which evidence is received does not establish procedural unfairness without a timely objection and resulting prejudice.
material_facts: Some evidence for the complainants was received after the advocate had given evidence.
The advocate did not complain about the order of evidence before the District Judge or the High Court.
The record disclosed no prejudice caused by the order in which the witnesses were examined.
issues.conclusion: The alleged procedural irregularity did not warrant interference because no timely complaint or prejudice was shown.
issues.legal_principle: A complaint about the order in which evidence is adduced does not justify setting aside a professional-misconduct proceeding where the issue was not raised before the inquiry court or the High Court and the record shows no prejudice.

rule.if: professional_discipline_inquiry and evidence_received_after_practitioner_testified and no_timely_objection and no_prejudice_shown

predicates.professional_discipline_inquiry: The proceeding is an inquiry into alleged professional misconduct.
predicates.evidence_received_after_practitioner_tes: Evidence for the complainant was received after the practitioner had testified.
predicates.no_timely_objection: The practitioner did not object to the order of evidence before the inquiry court or the court reviewing the inquiry.
predicates.no_prejudice_shown: The record does not show that the order of evidence caused prejudice to the practitioner.

issues.definition: In a professional-misconduct inquiry, receiving complainant evidence after the practitioner testifies does not invalidate the proceeding when no timely objection or resulting prejudice is shown.

issues.legal_issue: An advocate’s failure to account to clients for money received on their behalf, when coupled with a false claim of payment, establishes professional misconduct where the asserted evidence of payment is found unreliable.
material_facts: The advocate received and cashed a court cheque issued for money to which his clients were entitled.
The advocate did not dispute receiving the money on the clients’ behalf.
After the clients demanded the money, the advocate asserted that he had already paid it and that a receipt had been returned among the case papers.
The High Court found the witness said to support the payment defence to be an impersonator or, alternatively, wholly unworthy of belief.
The High Court found that the advocate had not paid the money to his clients.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the advocate failed to pay the money to his clients and was guilty of professional misconduct was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: A practitioner’s duty to a client includes properly accounting for money received on the client’s behalf. The High Court’s factual findings on whether payment was made and whether a witness was credible were not open to reappraisal by the Supreme Court in the absence of an exceptional ground for interference. The Court held that the witness’s asserted admission could not support the payment defence because the High Court had found the testimony devoid of truth.

rule.if: professional_misconduct_appeal and practitioner_received_client_money and clients_entitled_to_money and money_not_paid_to_clients and payment_witness_found_unreliable

predicates.professional_misconduct_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a finding of professional misconduct.
predicates.practitioner_received_client_money: The practitioner received money on behalf of clients in the course of professional work.
predicates.clients_entitled_to_money: The clients were entitled to receive the money held by the practitioner.
predicates.money_not_paid_to_clients: The practitioner did not pay the money to the clients despite their demand.
predicates.payment_witness_found_unreliable: The fact-finding court rejected as untruthful or unreliable the witness testimony offered to show that payment had been made.

issues.definition: When a practitioner received money for clients who were entitled to it, did not pay it to them, and the fact-finding court rejected the payment testimony as unreliable, the failure to account for the money is professional misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: A substantial suspension is not reduced when the misconduct involves withholding a considerable sum belonging to clients, falsely claiming payment, and attempting to support that claim through false evidence.
material_facts: The advocate held a considerable sum belonging to his clients and failed to repay it when they demanded payment.
The High Court found that the advocate put forward a false defence that he had paid the clients.
The High Court found that the advocate sought to support that defence by suborning witnesses.
The High Court suspended the advocate from practice for five years.
issues.conclusion: There was no justification for reducing the suspension; the punishment was, if anything, lenient given the gravity of the misconduct.
issues.legal_principle: The disciplinary court may impose a sanction proportionate to the gravity of professional misconduct. The Court considered withholding clients’ money, falsely asserting repayment, and seeking to sustain that defence through suborned witnesses sufficiently grave to justify the suspension imposed, and observed that striking the advocate from the roll could also have been a proper punishment.

predicates.appeal_challenging_professional_discipli: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reduction of a sanction imposed for professional misconduct.
predicates.practitioner_withheld_substantial_client: The practitioner retained a considerable sum belonging to clients and failed to return it when demanded.
predicates.practitioner_falsely_claimed_repayment: The practitioner asserted that the money had been repaid when the disciplinary court found that assertion false.
predicates.practitioner_used_suborned_witnesses: The disciplinary court found that the practitioner sought to support the false repayment claim by suborning witnesses.

issues.definition: When an appeal seeks reduction of a professional-discipline sanction for withholding substantial client money, falsely claiming repayment, and using suborned witnesses, the suspension is not reduced.
